haiti: Haiti forms the western three-eighths of Hispaniola, the second-largest island of the Greater Antilles, and shares a border of 360 km with the Dominican Republic. It is the most mountainous country in the Caribbean, with plains covering only 22% of its territory, and the highest point is Pic la Selle at 2,680 m. The name comes from the Taino language and means land of high mountains. It was the native name for the whole island, and Jean-Jacques Dessalines restored it as the official name of independent Saint-Domingue, in tribute to the Amerindian predecessors.

Indigenous peoples have lived on Hispaniola for about 6,000 years. Arawakan-speaking ancestors of the Taino arrived during the 1st millennium BCE, and at the time of European contact the island was divided among five caciquedoms led by chiefs. Christopher Columbus landed on 6 December 1492 and claimed the island for the Crown of Castile. The 39 men he left behind founded La Navidad but were later killed by the Taino.

European diseases caused epidemics among the native people, the first recorded smallpox epidemic in the Americas breaking out on Hispaniola in 1507, and the encomienda system, which forced natives to work in gold mines and plantations, reduced their numbers further. Spain held the island until 1697, when the western part was ceded to France as Saint-Domingue, a plantation colony worked by enslaved Africans.

The Haitian Revolution of 1791 to 1804 made Haiti the first sovereign state in the Caribbean and the first country in the Americas to abolish slavery officially. The independent state began as an empire, later split into two and reunited in 1820, and a second empire under Faustin Soulouque ended with the return of the republic in 1859. The 19th century brought instability, international isolation and a crippling debt to France. United States forces occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934, and the Duvalier family ruled as dictators from 1957 to 1986.

Haiti is a republic with Port-au-Prince as its capital and largest city, and about 11 million people, the most in the Caribbean. Its culture blends French and African customs with Spanish and Indigenous influences. The Citadelle Laferrière, built between 1805 and 1820, and the Sans-Souci Palace were inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1982.
hamburg: Hamburg lies at a sheltered natural harbour on the southern fanning-out of the Jutland Peninsula, between continental Europe to the south and Scandinavia to the north, with the North Sea to the west and the Baltic Sea to the northeast. It stands on the River Elbe at its confluence with the Alster and Bille, where the 110 km Elbe estuary begins. The city centre is around the Binnenalster and Außenalster, both lakes formed by damming the Alster. The Altes Land, part of the city, is the largest contiguous fruit-producing region in Central Europe.

Claudius Ptolemy, in the 2nd century CE, reported the first name for the vicinity as Treva. The name Hamburg comes from the first permanent building on the site, a castle which Charlemagne ordered built in 808. It rose on rocky terrain in a marsh between the Alster and the Elbe as a defence against Slavic incursion and acquired the name Hammaburg, burg meaning castle or fort.

In 834 Hamburg became the seat of a bishopric, whose first bishop, Ansgar, later known as the Apostle of the North, founded the city's early Christian institutions. Two years later it was linked with Bremen to form the Bishopric of Hamburg-Bremen. The town was destroyed repeatedly in its early centuries. In 845 a fleet of 600 Viking ships sailed up the Elbe and destroyed it, when it had about 500 inhabitants. King Mieszko II Lambert of Poland burned it in 1030, and Valdemar II of Denmark raided and occupied it in 1201 and 1214. The Black Death reached Hamburg in 1350 and killed at least 60 per cent of its population, and the city suffered several major fires in the medieval period.

Hamburg was a member of the Hanseatic League and a free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire. Before the unification of Germany in 1871 it was a fully sovereign city state, and before 1919 it was a civic republic headed constitutionally by a class of hereditary Grand Burghers, or Hanseaten. Later disasters included the Great Fire of 1842, the Allied fire-bombing of 1943 and the North Sea flood of 1962.

Officially the Free and Hanseatic City of Hamburg, it is the second-largest city in Germany after Berlin and one of the country's three city-states, with Berlin and Bremen. Its population is over 1.9 million. The Port of Hamburg is Germany's largest. The Speicherstadt and Kontorhausviertel were declared World Heritage Sites by UNESCO in 2015.
hanoi: Hanoi lies on the Red River, whose curved course around the city was symbolised as a dragon. Several of the city's older names contain the Chinese word for dragon: it was first called Long Biên, then Tống Bình and Long Đỗ, and after its recapture in 866 by the Tang general Gao Pian it was renamed Đại La. Medieval Muslim sources between the 9th and 12th century called it Luqin, a term derived from Longbian.

Stone tools of the Sơn Vi culture, 10,000 to 20,000 years old, have been found at Ba Vì and Đông Anh. From about 10,000 to 4,000 years ago the area was under water as the sea rose, and the region is believed to have been inhabited continuously for the last 4,000 years.

Around the third century BCE a fortified citadel, later named Cổ Loa, was built in the area; it was the first political centre of the Vietnamese civilisation before Chinese influence, with an outer embankment covering 600 hectares. In 179 BCE Nanyue annexed the region, and Zhao Tuo left the indigenous chiefs in control of the population. For the first time the area formed part of a polity headed by a Chinese ruler.

In 1010, under the Lý dynasty, Emperor Lý Thái Tổ established the capital of Đại Việt in what later became central Hanoi and named it Thăng Long, meaning ascending dragon. In 1428 King Lê Lợi renamed it Đông Kinh, eastern capital, a name used until 1789. In 1802 the Nguyễn dynasty moved the national capital to Huế, and the city was renamed Hanoi in 1831. The French took control in 1888 and shaped the city's architecture to their tastes. Hanoi was the capital of the French protectorate of Tonkin from 1883 to 1949 and of French Indochina from 1902 to 1945. Ernest Hebrard drew up a development plan in 1924, which was partly carried out.

After the August Revolution and the fall of the Nguyễn dynasty, the Democratic Republic of Vietnam made Hanoi its capital. The city was part of the State of Vietnam from 1949 to 1954 and again of the Democratic Republic from 1954 to 1976. In 1976 it became the capital of the unified Socialist Republic of Vietnam.

Hanoi is the capital and second most populous centrally governed city of Vietnam, with about 8.7 million people. Its Old Quarter, near Hoàn Kiếm Lake, keeps most of its original street layout, descended from the 36 streets where merchants specialised in trades such as silk, jewellery or bamboo. The city also holds the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long, the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum and the French colonial Hanoi Opera House and St. Joseph's Cathedral. UNESCO gave Hanoi the title City for Peace on 16 July 1999.
hans-christian-andersen: Hans Christian Andersen was born in Odense on 2 April 1805. His father, also named Hans, had an elementary school education and introduced his son to literature by reading him the Arabian Nights; his mother, Anne Marie Andersdatter, was an illiterate washerwoman. After his father's death in 1816 the boy attended a local school for poor children and had to support himself, working as an apprentice to a weaver and later to a tailor.

At 14 he moved to Copenhagen to seek work as an actor and was accepted into the Royal Danish Theatre for his soprano voice, which soon broke. A colleague told him he considered him a poet, and Andersen turned to writing. Jonas Collin, the theatre's director, persuaded King Frederick VI to pay part of his schooling at Slagelse and later Elsinore, which lasted until 1827.

His first story, "The Ghost at Palnatoke's Grave", appeared in 1822. In 1829 he had considerable success with the short story "A Journey on Foot from Holmen's Canal to the East Point of Amager", followed by a play and a short volume of poems. A small travel grant from the king in 1833 let him begin the first of many journeys through Europe, and he reached Rome in October 1834. His travels in Italy shaped his first novel, The Improvisatore, a fictionalized autobiography published in 1835 to instant acclaim.

Andersen's first fairy tales were issued in three booklets by C. A. Reitzel in Copenhagen between May 1835 and April 1837. The first, of 8 May 1835, held "The Tinderbox", "Little Claus and Big Claus", "The Princess and the Pea" and "Little Ida's Flowers"; the first three were based on folktales he had heard in childhood. In June 1847 he visited England and met Charles Dickens. In 1857 he stayed five weeks at Dickens's home, Gads Hill Place, after which Dickens stopped writing to him, which Andersen never understood.

In early 1872 Andersen fell out of his bed and was severely hurt, and soon afterwards he showed signs of liver cancer. He died on 4 August 1875 at Rolighed, a country house near Copenhagen belonging to his friends Moritz G. Melchior and his wife. By then he was internationally revered, and the Danish government paid him an annual stipend as a national treasure. His 156 fairy tales in nine volumes have been translated into more than 125 languages and have inspired ballets, plays and films.
harry-s-truman: Harry S. Truman was born in Lamar, Missouri, on 8 May 1884, the oldest child of John Anderson Truman and Martha Ellen Young Truman. His middle initial honours both his grandfathers and is not an abbreviation of one name. His father was a farmer and livestock dealer, and the family settled in Independence, Missouri, when Harry was six. He was refused an appointment to West Point because of poor eyesight and served in the Missouri National Guard from 1905 to 1911.

When the United States entered World War I on 6 April 1917, Truman rejoined his battery and fought in France as a captain in the Field Artillery. In 1919 he married Bess Wallace. He and Edward Jacobson opened a haberdashery in Kansas City, which went bankrupt in the recession of 1921.

Truman was elected a judge of Jackson County in 1922 and a senator for Missouri in 1934. From 1940 to 1944 he gained national prominence as chairman of the Truman Committee, which aimed to reduce waste and inefficiency in wartime contracts. He was nominated as Franklin D. Roosevelt's running mate, though reluctant, and was sworn in as vice president on 20 January 1945. He became president on Roosevelt's death in April. Only then was he told about the Manhattan Project and the atomic bomb.

As president Truman authorized the use of nuclear weapons against the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, set up the Marshall Plan and established the Truman Doctrine. He supported the founding of NATO and presided over the onset of the Cold War in 1947 and the Berlin Airlift in 1948. When Congress refused his proposal for comprehensive civil rights legislation, he issued orders that prohibited discrimination in federal agencies and desegregated the armed forces. He won the 1948 election against Thomas E. Dewey. The Korean War lasted from 1950 to 1953. Corruption in parts of his administration, which did not implicate Truman himself, became a campaign issue in 1952, and he chose not to run again.

In retirement Truman founded his presidential library and published his memoirs. He was admitted to hospital in Kansas City with pneumonia on 5 December 1972, developed multiple organ failure and died on 26 December, aged 88. When he left office in 1953 his administration was heavily criticised, but public feeling towards him grew warmer over the following decades.
harsha-of-kashmir: Harsha, also called Harshadeva, was born in 1059, the son of King Kalasha of Kashmir. Almost everything known of him comes from the Rajatarangini of Kalhana, whose father Champaka had been one of Harsha's ministers and who wrote in the time of Jayasimha, between 1127 and 1159. According to Kalhana he was built like a god and extremely handsome. He is said to have begun as a capable and noble king before his spending brought him into financial trouble.

Extravagant outlay on his troops and on pleasures left the king in grave difficulties. The historian Prithvi Nath Kaul Bamzai notes Kalhana's statement that even night soil was taxed. An accidental discovery of hoarded treasure at the Bhimasahi temple led him to despoil other temples and to melt down gold and silver images. Kalhana writes that not one temple kept its images, and that only two chief divine images were respected, Ranaswamin in the city and Martanda. Two colossal statues of the Buddha were saved by requests made one at Parihasapura by the singer Kanaka and one in the city by the monk Kusalsri.

Kalhana calls him that Turushka, and he bore the epithet raja-Turushka, Turk king. Turkish troops served him as mercenaries, and the chronicle says he continually supported Turushka captains-of-hundreds with money, while adding that he ate domesticated pigs until his death. According to the historian André Wink, Harsha in all likelihood took up the Muslim tradition of iconoclasm, as the epithet indicates. Kalhana also charges him with credulity towards parasites at court, who passed off slave girls as goddesses, and with incest with his sisters and violence against Naga, his father's sister's daughter.

Harsha died on 31 August 1101, the last ruler of the First Lohara dynasty. His conduct has remained a subject of discussion. The great Buddha of the capital outlived him: Kalhana records that when a fire reduced the city to a heap of earth in the reign of Sussala, the statue alone stood visible, blackened by smoke. The statue at Parihasapura had been made by Lalitaditya Muktapida, and Abul-Fazl states that the temples of that place were finally destroyed by Sikandar Butshikan, who ruled from 1389 to 1413.
havana: Havana lies on the northern coast of Cuba along the Straits of Florida, south of the Florida Keys, where the Gulf of Mexico joins the Atlantic Ocean. The city extends mostly westward and southward from a bay, which is entered through a narrow inlet and divides into three main harbours. The Almendares River crosses the city from south to north.

The city stands mostly on low hills. A limestone ridge about 60 metres high slopes up from the east and culminates in the heights of La Cabaña and El Morro, where the Spanish built fortifications overlooking the eastern bay.

In the early 16th century Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar founded the town of San Cristóbal de la Habana on the southern coast of Cuba, at the mouth of the Mayabeque River, now the town of Batabanó. The low and swampy land caused the settlement to fail. In those years the Spanish established settlements on the northern coast, among them La Chorrera, at the mouth of the Almendares River. The town that became Havana grew up beside Puerto de Carenas, the Careening Port, in 1519, and the quality of the harbour led to the change of location.

Havana overtook Santiago in the mid-16th century because of the advantages of its harbour and became the capital of the island. It became a fundamental place for the Spanish colonial empire in the Americas and a stopping point for galleons returning to the Iberian Peninsula, and walls and forts were built to protect it from naval attacks. After the Cuban War of Independence a new constitution was adopted in 1901.

Havana is the capital and largest city of Cuba and the seat of its government. It is the country's main port. The population in 2021 was 2,142,939. Its economy first developed on its location as one of the early great trade centres of the New World, and sugar and a slave trade first brought riches to the city.

Old Havana, Habana Vieja, contains the core of the original city and was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982. Its landmarks include the Fortress San Carlos de la Cabaña, El Morro Castle, built because of the threat to the harbour from pirates, and the Fortress San Salvador de la Punta, built in the 16th century. The University of Havana was established in 1728.
hawaii: Hawaii consists of 137 volcanic islands that make up almost the entire Hawaiian archipelago, spanning 1,500 miles in the Pacific Ocean about 2,000 miles southwest of the U.S. mainland. The eight main islands, from northwest to southeast, are Niʻihau, Kauaʻi, Oʻahu, Molokaʻi, Lānaʻi, Kahoʻolawe, Maui and Hawaiʻi, after which the state is named. The archipelago is physiographically and ethnologically part of Polynesia. The name Hawaiʻi is very similar to Proto-Polynesian *Sawaiki, reconstructed as meaning homeland, and one explanation names it for Hawaiʻiloa, a figure of oral tradition said to have discovered the islands.

The date of human arrival is debated. Early archaeological studies suggested Polynesians from the Marquesas or Society Islands arrived as early as the 3rd century CE. Some archaeologists think a later wave from Tahiti around 1100 CE introduced a new line of high chiefs, the kapu system, human sacrifice and the building of heiau, as Hawaiian tradition tells of Paʻao. Others say no evidence supports a later influx and treat Paʻao as myth, and more recent studies place the first settlement at around 900 to 1200 CE. The islands were home to numerous independent chiefdoms.

In 1778 the British explorer James Cook was the first known non-Polynesian to arrive. European and American explorers, traders and whalers followed, and introduced diseases such as syphilis, tuberculosis, smallpox and measles. The indigenous population fell from an estimated 300,000 in the 1770s to 60,000 in the 1850s and 24,000 in 1920, though estimates of the pre-contact figure range from 150,000 to 1.5 million. Hawaii became a unified, internationally recognised kingdom in 1810.

Sugar plantations had a strong foothold by the 1840s and were tightly controlled by American missionary families and businessmen known as the Big Five. In 1893 resident American and European capitalists and landholders overthrew the monarchy. Hawaii was an independent republic from 1894 until 12 August 1898, when it became a U.S. territory. It was attacked by Japan on 7 December 1941 and admitted as a state on 21 August 1959. In 1993 the U.S. government formally apologised for its role in the overthrow.

Hawaii is the 50th state of the United States, with its capital and largest city, Honolulu, on Oʻahu, where two thirds of residents live. Hawaiian was added to the state constitution in 1978 as an official language alongside English. Kamehameha III chose Honolulu as capital for its natural harbour, the present-day Honolulu Harbor, and the previous capitals were Lahaina on Maui and Kailua-Kona on Hawaiʻi. The aboriginal culture is Polynesian, and lūʻau and hula have spread in modified form to the wider United States.
hawiye: The Hawiye trace their lineage to Sheikh Ahmed bin Abdulrahman bin Uthman, known as Sheikh Hawiye. Oral tradition and Arabic hagiologies remember him as a saint called Hawi al-Ulum, conservator of knowledge, a name shortened in time to Hawiye, and carry his genealogy back to Aqeel bin Abu Talib. Some scholars regard such claims as historically untenable. The anthropologist Ioan Lewis held that traditions of descent from noble Arab families are most probably figurative expressions of the importance of Islam in Somali society. Tradition places his tomb at Qundhuro in the Haraghe region, where his eldest son Karanle is buried beside him.

The 12th-century writer Al-Idrisi placed the Hawiye on the coast between Ras Hafun and Merca and in the lower basin of the Shabelle river, the first documentary reference to a specific Somali group. Ibn Sa'id, who lived from 1214 to 1274, called Merca their capital.

In the 13th century the Hawiye, with the Rahanweyn, came under the Ajuran Empire, whose domain reached from Hobyo in the north to Qelafo in the west and Kismayo in the south. The Ajuran are themselves said to descend from the Jambelle branch of the Hawiye, and Lee Cassanelli describes Ajuran power as resting on spiritual pre-eminence and Hawiye kinship solidarity.

According to local oral tradition as Cassanelli reports it, the Hiraab Imamate was an alliance of closely related groups of the Gorgaarte division. Its founders rebelled because the Ajuran rulers had grown proud, neglected sharia law and imposed heavy taxes. With Mogadishu as its capital, the imamate ruled from the Shabelle valley and the Benadir to the arid lands of Mudug for at least two centuries. The explorer John Kirk, visiting in 1873, met Imam Mahmood at Mogadishu and saw about twenty large dhows there and at Merca loading grain, much of it for Zanzibar.

At independence in 1960 the first president, Aden Adde, the first prime minister, Abdullahi Issa, and the founder of the army, Daud Abdulle Hirsi, were all Hawiye. Hawiye leaders formed the United Somali Congress in opposition to President Siad Barre, whom General Mohamed Farrah Aidid, of the Habar Gidir, overthrew in 1991. From late 1991 Mogadishu was divided between the factions of Aidid and of President Ali Mahdi Muhammad, of the Abgaal. The stalemate lasted until 2006, when the Islamic Courts Union, a predominantly Hawiye organisation, ended the rule of the factional warlords, before an Ethiopian intervention overthrew it. The Hiraab hereditary leadership survives to this day.
hebrew: Hebrew is a Northwest Semitic language and belongs to the Canaanite languages. It was the spoken language of the Iron Age kingdoms of Israel and Judah from about 1200 to 586 BCE, and epigraphic evidence supports the view that the earlier layers of biblical literature reflect their language. The earliest examples of written Paleo-Hebrew date to the 10th century BCE. Two claims for older inscriptions are disputed: Amihai Mazar called a shard from Khirbet Qeiyafa, which its discoverer Yossi Garfinkel thought might be the earliest Hebrew writing, proto-Canaanite, and a claimed curse tablet from Mount Ebal is rejected by practically all professional epigraphers apart from its discoverer's team.

Nearly all the Hebrew Bible is written in Biblical Hebrew, much of it in a dialect that scholars believe flourished around the 6th century BCE. For this reason Jews have called it Lashon Hakodesh, 'the holy tongue', since ancient times. The Bible itself calls it Yehudit, 'Judean', and the name Ivrit appears in the Mishnah. Hebrew is written from right to left in an abjad of 22 letters. The ancient Paleo-Hebrew alphabet resembled the Canaanite and Phoenician ones, while the modern 'square' script, Ashurit, developed from the Aramaic script.

Scholars debate how far Hebrew remained a spoken vernacular after the Babylonian exile, when Old Aramaic was the predominant international language. It ceased to be a regular spoken language between 200 and 400 CE, as it declined after the unsuccessful Bar Kokhba revolt against the Roman Empire. It survived as the language of Jewish liturgy, rabbinic literature, commerce between Jews of different native languages and poetry. The first dated book printed in Hebrew was published by Abraham Garton in Reggio in 1475. With the rise of Zionism in the 19th century it was revived as a spoken language, led by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, and Modern Hebrew became the main language of the Yishuv in Palestine and then the official language of the State of Israel.
herodotus: Herodotus was, by his own statement at the beginning of his work, a native of Halicarnassus in Anatolia, and it is generally accepted that he was born there in the early fifth century BCE. The Suda, a Byzantine encyclopaedia of the 10th century, says that his family was influential, that he was the son of Lyxes and Dryo and that he was related to the epic poet Panyassis. Since Lyxes and Panyassis are Carian names, he was probably at least partly a Hellenised Carian. Halicarnassus was within the Persian Empire, which made him a Persian subject.

The evidence for his life is slight and late. According to the Suda he learned the Ionian dialect on Samos, to which his family fled from the tyrant Lygdamis, and later returned to lead the revolt that overthrew him. Inscriptions show that Ionic Greek was used in official documents at Halicarnassus, and since the Suda is the only source for the liberation, its account is doubtful.

Herodotus's eyewitness accounts indicate that he travelled in Egypt in association with Athenians, probably after 454 BCE. He probably went to Tyre next and then down the Euphrates to Babylon. For some reason he became unpopular in Halicarnassus and around 447 BCE migrated to Athens, whose people and democratic institutions he openly admired. In 443 BCE or shortly afterwards he moved to Thurii, in modern Calabria, as part of an Athenian-sponsored colony.

He made his researches known through oral recitations. According to Lucian he read the whole of the Histories at the Olympic Games in one sitting. The work deals chiefly with the lives of prominent kings and with battles such as Marathon, Thermopylae, Artemisium, Salamis, Plataea and Mycale, and digresses into cultural, ethnographic and geographical background. Nothing in it can be dated with certainty to later than 430 BCE.

The place of his death is unknown. He may have returned to Athens and died there in the plague, or died in Macedonia or at Thurii. His is the earliest Greek prose work to survive intact. Cicero called him the Father of History, but his many strange stories and folk-tales led critics to brand him the Father of Lies. Thucydides dismissed him as a story-teller. Herodotus answered that he reported what he could see and what he was told.
himalayas: The Himalayas run west-northwest to east-southeast in an arc 2,400 km long, between the Indo-Gangetic Plain in the south and the Tibetan Plateau in the north. Nanga Parbat anchors the western end, near the northernmost bend of the Indus, and Namcha Barwa the eastern end, near the great bend of the Yarlung Tsangpo. The range is 350 km wide in the west and 151 km in the east. It consists of four parallel ranges from south to north: the Sivalik Hills, the Lower Himalayan Range, the Great Himalayas, which is the highest and central range, and the Tibetan Himalayas. More than 100 peaks exceed 7,200 metres, and the Mahalangur Himal holds four of the world's six highest mountains, including Everest.

The mountains were uplifted after the Indian tectonic plate collided with the Eurasian plate. India had begun to split away from Gondwana about 70 million years ago and moved north. Its thick, buoyant continental plate could not subduct, and the upper crust piled up in sheets called nappes. The geophysicist Peter Molnar noted that most of the Himalayas are slices of rock that once were the top part of India's crust.

The Himalayas span Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan, and the sovereignty of the range in Kashmir is disputed. The Indus, the Ganges and the Tsangpo–Brahmaputra rise in the range, and their drainage basin is home to some 600 million people, while 53 million live in the Himalayas themselves. The range holds about 15,000 glaciers and is sometimes called the Third Pole. Kathmandu, the capital of Nepal, is the largest city in the Himalayas. The snow leopard is the main predator at high altitudes, and the red panda lives in the bamboo forests of the eastern Himalayas.

The name comes from the Sanskrit Himālaya, abode of snow. The range has profoundly shaped the cultures of South Asia and Tibet. For Hindus the Himalayas are personified as Himavat, king of the mountains and father of the goddess Parvati, and the temples at Pashupatinath and Muktinath are major pilgrimage places. Muktinath is also a pilgrimage place for Tibetan Buddhists, and Paro Taktsang is where Padmasambhava is said to have founded Buddhism in Bhutan. In Jainism, Mount Ashtapada is where the first tirthankara, Rishabhanatha, attained moksha. The summits of several peaks, including Nanda Devi and Gangkhar Puensum, are off limits to climbers.
hiv-aids: HIV is a retrovirus of the genus Lentivirus, in the family Retroviridae. It infects components of the human immune system, chiefly CD4+ T cells, macrophages and dendritic cells, and destroys CD4+ T cells directly and indirectly. Infection passes through three main stages: an acute stage, often an influenza-like illness two to four weeks after exposure; a long period of clinical latency; and AIDS, when the risk of tuberculosis, other opportunistic infections and rare tumours rises. Without treatment, average survival after infection is estimated at nine to eleven years.

The virus is spread by sexual contact, by significant exposure to infected body fluids or tissues, such as contaminated needles or blood transfusions, and from mother to child during pregnancy, delivery or breastfeeding. Saliva, sweat, tears and urine carry no risk unless they are contaminated with blood. Most infected people develop antibodies within three to twelve weeks of infection.

HIV made the jump from other primates to humans in west-central Africa in the early to mid-20th century. The first news story on the disease appeared on 18 May 1981 in the gay newspaper New York Native, and on 5 June 1981 AIDS was first clinically reported, with five cases in the United States. The patients were injecting drug users and gay men who showed symptoms of Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia, a rare infection of people with badly impaired immunity. Many cases of the skin cancer Kaposi's sarcoma followed, and the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention formed a task force to monitor the outbreak. The cause, HIV infection, was identified in the early part of the decade.

The disease had a large impact on society, both as an illness and as a source of discrimination. Stigma took the forms of ostracism, rejection, compulsory testing without consent, violence and quarantine, and the fear of it kept many people from seeking testing or treatment. The disease was also drawn into controversies involving religion, among them the Catholic Church's position not to support condom use as prevention.

Antiretroviral therapy changed the prognosis. It reduces the death rate by 80% and raises the life expectancy of a newly diagnosed young adult to between 20 and 50 years. A person with an undetectable viral load as a result of long-term treatment has effectively no risk of transmitting HIV sexually, a finding publicised in the Swiss Statement of 2008 and since accepted as medically sound. Annual deaths from the disease peaked at 2 million in 2005.
ho-chi-minh-city: Ho Chi Minh City lies in south-east Vietnam on the Mekong Delta, and its geography is defined by rivers and canals, the largest being the Saigon River. The centre stands about 5 metres above sea level, and the city is fringed by tidal flats that have been altered for agriculture. It has a coast 89 kilometres long on the South China Sea. In the rainy season, tides, rain, river flow and land subsidence together flood parts of the city.

The first known settlement was a Cham one called Baigaur. The Khmer renamed it Prey Nokôr, a fishing village, and Vietnamese settlers in the early 17th century took over the Khmer name as Sài Gòn. It was officially renamed Gia Định in 1698. The name Ho Chi Minh City was given in 1976, after reunification, to honour Ho Chi Minh. Sài Gòn remains in everyday speech and refers to the city centre.

An early Funan temple, said to be the site of the later Phụng Sơn Buddhist temple, was founded in the 4th century CE, and a Champa settlement dates to the 11th century. The Khmer Empire took Baigaur around 1145. In 1620 Princess Nguyễn Phúc Ngọc Vạn, daughter of Lord Nguyễn Phúc Nguyên, married King Chey Chettha II of Cambodia, which eased relations and let people of the two countries move freely. Chey Chettha II in exchange gave Prei Nokor to the Nguyễn lords.

After the fall of the Citadel of Saigon in the Cochinchina campaign in 1859, the city was the capital of French Cochinchina from 1862 to 1949. It was capital of French Indochina from 1887 to 1902 and again from 1945 to 1954, and of the State of Vietnam from 1949 to 1955. After the 1954 partition it was the capital of South Vietnam until its capture by North Vietnam, which led to a unified state in 1976.

Ho Chi Minh City is the most populous city of Vietnam, with more than 14 million people after the merger of Bình Dương and Bà Rịa-Vũng Tàu into it in 2025. French colonial buildings such as the City Hall, the Saigon Central Post Office and the Notre-Dame Cathedral Basilica stand in the centre. The Thien Hau Temple, first built around 1760, is in the Chinese quarter of Chợ Lớn, and the Independence Palace dates from the era of the Republic of Vietnam.
hoelun: Most of what is known of Hö'elün comes from the Secret History of the Mongols, a mid-13th-century epic that is very favourable to her; its anonymous author probably had links to her. According to it she was born into the Olkhonud clan of the Onggirat tribe and was married at around fifteen, in about 1160 or 1161, to Chiledu, brother of the Merkit chief. On the journey to his lands the couple were ambushed by Mongols out hawking, led by Yesügei of the Borjigin clan. The kidnapping, omitted from most official chronicles, left a grudge among the Merkit that later became a blood feud.

Yesügei already had a wife, usually named Sochigel by historians, and a son, Behter, but Hö'elün became his primary wife. She bore him four sons, Temüjin, Qasar, Hachiun and Temüge, and a daughter, Temülen. The year of Temüjin's birth is disputed, with 1155, 1162 and 1167 each favoured by different historians.

Yesügei was poisoned by Tatars when Temüjin was about eight. The Tayichiud faction excluded Hö'elün from the ancestor ceremonies and abandoned her camp. The Secret History says the whole Borjigin clan followed, though other sources, such as the Persian historian Rashid al-Din, imply that Yesügei's brothers stood by her. When Temüjin and Qasar ambushed and killed Behter, the Secret History has her angrily reprimand them.

After Temüjin married Börte, the two women managed the economy of his camp, and he turned to them first for counsel when he split from Jamuqa. After his defeat at Dalan Balzhut in 1187, Hö'elün married Münglig, an old retainer of Yesügei, in her third and final marriage. In the following years she probably arranged marriages for her youngest children and maintained alliances while Temüjin was away. The Secret History says she raised numerous foundlings, but problems of chronology indicate that the best known, Shigi Qutuqu, was in fact raised by Börte.

At the assembly of 1206 Hö'elün was reportedly granted 10,000 followers jointly with Temüge, and felt that this undervalued her work; Münglig, by contrast, received the seat at the khan's right hand. When Münglig's son, the shaman Kokechu, divided Genghis Khan from his brothers, she defended Qasar and Temüge vigorously, and with Börte persuaded Genghis that Kokechu must be eliminated. The Secret History claims that she died soon after, worn out by her efforts, an account that some historians, such as Igor de Rachewiltz, have called poetical melodrama. By the time of the Yuan dynasty she had received the posthumous name Empress Xuanyi.
holocaust: Jews have lived in Europe for more than two thousand years. Throughout the Middle Ages they were subjected to antisemitism based on Christian theology, which blamed them for killing Jesus. In the 19th century many European countries granted Jews full citizenship, and political antisemitism, positing an international Jewish conspiracy, emerged with the rise of nationalism and industrialization. After the First World War the German military promoted the untrue idea that Germany had been stabbed in the back by socialists and Jews.

Adolf Hitler was appointed chancellor in January 1933. Within months all other parties were banned and tens of thousands of political opponents arrested. The regime passed anti-Jewish laws, encouraged violence and orchestrated the nationwide pogrom known as Kristallnacht in November 1938, meaning to force all German Jews to emigrate.

After Germany invaded Poland in September 1939, the occupation authorities began to establish ghettos to segregate Jews. Following the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941, German forces and local collaborators murdered 1.5 to 2 million Jews. Most historians agree that Hitler issued an explicit order to kill all Jews in Europe, but disagree about when. Reinhard Heydrich convened the Wannsee Conference on 20 January 1942, and the Final Solution was implemented to murder all Jews in Europe.

Victims were deported to extermination camps, chiefly Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Belzec, Sobibor, Chełmno and Majdanek in occupied Poland, where those who survived the journey were gassed. Others were sent to forced labour camps, where many died of starvation, abuse and exhaustion. The murder rate was highest during Operation Reinhard, from March 1942 to November 1943. In 1944 about 437,000 Hungarian Jews were deported in eight weeks, mostly to Auschwitz. The killings continued until 1945.

Around six million Jews were killed, about two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population. Half of the victims came from Poland. Many survivors emigrated from Europe after the war, and the Kielce pogrom convinced many that they could not stay in eastern Europe. Relatively few perpetrators faced criminal trials, and billions of dollars in reparations have been paid, though they fall short of the losses suffered. The Holocaust is considered the largest genocide in human history and has become central to Western historical consciousness.
homer: The identity of Homer is a mystery, and scholars generally regard the ancient picture of a single author behind the Iliad and the Odyssey as a fictional narrative. Their composition is thought to date to the late eighth or early seventh century BCE. Many accounts of his life circulated in antiquity. The most widespread made him a blind bard from Ionia, a region including the central west coast of Anatolia and the islands of Chios and Samos, but modern scholars regard these accounts as apocryphal. The earliest implicit references to Homer, in the 7th century BCE, are in works by Archilochus, Alcman, Tyrtaeus and Callinus.

Pindar is credited with saying that Homer came from Chios and Smyrna. The historian Ephorus held that he studied poetry with the bard Phemius and was born in Cyme, Philochorus thought Argos was his birthplace, and later writers believed it was Pylos or Athens. The Byzantine Suda described him as descended from a Muse, Apollo, Orpheus or others. No account of his origin became mainstream, but most place his death on the island of Ios, where two epigrams by Alcaeus of Messene commemorate his burial.

The Iliad centres on a quarrel between King Agamemnon and the warrior Achilles in the last year of the Trojan War. The Odyssey chronicles the ten-year journey home of Odysseus, king of Ithaca, after the fall of Troy. Both are in Homeric Greek, a literary language mixing Ionic and Aeolic features, and are composed in unrhymed dactylic hexameters. Most researchers believe they were first transmitted orally, and set phrases such as crafty Odysseus and rosy-fingered Dawn aided the bard. Both begin with an invocation to the Muse.

The poems were put into written form between the eighth and sixth centuries BCE. Ancient tradition held that Pisistratus collected them in Athens in the late sixth century BCE. After the 24 books were fixed, scholars at Alexandria such as Aristarchus of Samothrace helped establish a canonical text.

The Homeric poems were widely used as school texts in Greek and Hellenistic cultures, the first literary works taught to all students. Plato said that Homer had educated Greece. Interpreters, especially the Stoics, read the poems as allegories containing hidden wisdom. The first printed edition was produced in Florence in 1488 by Demetrios Chalkokondyles. In 1873 Heinrich Schliemann announced the discovery of Homer's Troy at Hisarlik in modern Turkey.

Ancient chronology dated the sack of Troy to 1184 BCE, and some scholars think the destruction of Troy VIIa around 1220 BCE gave rise to the myth. The poems depict customs from different periods: their heroes use bronze weapons but are cremated, an Iron Age practice. Virgil's Aeneid was heavily influenced by Homer, and later works from Tennyson's Ulysses to James Joyce's Ulysses retell his stories.
hong-kong: Hong Kong is situated on China's southern coast, 60 kilometres east of Macau and on the eastern side of the Pearl River estuary. It is surrounded by the South China Sea on all sides except the north, where it neighbours the city of Shenzhen along the Sham Chun River. The territory consists of Hong Kong Island, the Kowloon Peninsula, the New Territories, Lantau Island and over 200 other islands. Its highest point is Tai Mo Shan, at 957 metres, and about 70 square kilometres of its land has been reclaimed from the sea.

The name was first romanised as He-Ong-Kong in 1780 and originally referred to a small inlet between Aberdeen Island and the southern coast of Hong Kong Island. It is generally believed to be an early phonetic rendering of a Cantonese phrase meaning 'fragrant harbour' or 'incense harbour'. The second colonial governor, Sir John Davis, offered an alternative origin, 'red torrent'. The name was often written as one word, Hongkong, until 1926, when the government officially adopted two words.

The earliest known human traces date to 35,000 to 39,000 years ago, based on knapped stone tools found at Wong Tei Tung in the Sai Kung Peninsula. About 6,000 years ago the region was widely occupied, and rice cultivation had been introduced by the Late Neolithic. The Qin dynasty incorporated the area into China for the first time in 214 BCE, after conquering the indigenous Baiyue. After the Qin collapsed it was consolidated under the Nanyue kingdom, and China recaptured it after the Han conquest. During the Mongol conquest in the 13th century the southern Song court was briefly located at the Sung Wong Toi site in Kowloon City, before its defeat at the Battle of Yamen in 1279.

The Qing dynasty ceded Hong Kong Island to the British Empire in 1841 to 1842 after losing the First Opium War. The colony expanded to the Kowloon Peninsula in 1860, and in 1898 the United Kingdom obtained a 99-year lease of the New Territories. Japan occupied Hong Kong from 1941 to 1945 during the Second World War. The territory was handed over from the United Kingdom to China in 1997.

Hong Kong is a special administrative region of China. Under the principle of one country, two systems and the Sino-British Joint Declaration, its Basic Law serves as the regional constitution, and it keeps separate governing and economic systems from those of mainland China. Its population was estimated at 7,413,070 in 2021, the great majority of them Chinese. Its culture is described as a hybrid of Eastern and Western influences.
honolulu: Honolulu lies along the southeast coast of the island of Oʻahu in the Pacific Ocean. The name is Hawaiian for sheltered harbour or calm port, and the old name of the area, Kou, roughly covers the heart of the present downtown district. It is the most remote major city in the United States and one of the most isolated in the world: the nearest point on the mainland, Point Arena Lighthouse in northern California, is 2,045 nautical miles away, and the nearest major city is San Francisco. The volcanic field of the Honolulu Volcanics lies partly within the city.

Oral histories and artifacts indicate that there was a settlement where Honolulu now stands in the 11th century, founded by the original Polynesian migrants to the archipelago. After Kamehameha I conquered Oʻahu in the Battle of Nuʻuanu at Nuʻuanu Pali, he moved his royal court from the island of Hawaiʻi to Waikiki in 1804, and in 1809 to what is now downtown Honolulu. The capital moved back to Kailua-Kona in 1812.

The geography of the area and Honolulu Harbor made it desirable as a port, which accounts for the city's growth and importance in the Hawaiian archipelago and the broader Pacific. Honolulu has been the capital of Hawaii since 1845, first as seat of the independent Hawaiian Kingdom until its overthrow in 1893, then of the United States territory established after annexation in 1898, and since 1959 of the state of Hawaii. The city gained worldwide recognition after the Empire of Japan attacked nearby Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, which brought the United States into the Second World War.

Honolulu is the capital and most populous city of Hawaii and the seat of the consolidated City and County of Honolulu. Pearl Harbor remains a major United States Navy base and hosts the United States Pacific Fleet. The Bishop Museum has the world's largest collection of Hawaiiana and Pacific culture artifacts, and ʻIolani Palace and the USS Arizona Memorial are among the city's sights.
hungary: Hungary is a landlocked country in Central Europe that spans much of the Carpathian Basin. It is bordered by Slovakia to the north, Ukraine to the northeast, Romania to the east and southeast, Serbia to the south, Croatia and Slovenia to the southwest, and Austria to the west. The whole country lies within the drainage basin of the Danube, which flows north to south through its centre. Its traditional divisions are Transdanubia, the land between the Danube and the Tisza, and the land beyond the Tisza.

Transdanubia is mostly hilly, with the eastern edge of the Alps in the west and Lake Balaton, the largest lake in Central Europe. The Great Hungarian Plain covers most of the east and southeast. Kékes, at 1,014 metres, is the tallest mountain, in the foothills of the Carpathians near the Slovak border.

The Roman Empire took the land west of the Danube in 16 to 15 BCE, and Pannonia was recognised as Roman in 14 BCE. The province of Dacia, which included the east of present-day Hungary, was formed in 106 CE and remained under Roman rule until 271. Later arrivals included the Hunnic Empire (c. 370 to 469), the Gepids, and the Avars, who founded the Avar Khaganate in the 560s. The Franks under Charlemagne defeated the Avars in a series of campaigns during the 790s.

Statehood began in the late ninth century with the Principality of Hungary, which became a Christian kingdom under King Stephen I in 1000. After the Battle of Mohács in 1526 the kingdom was divided into three regions for over 150 years, until it was reunited under Habsburg rule before the turn of the 18th century. The Treaty of Trianon in 1920 set Hungary's modern borders and cost it 71% of its historical territory; a third of ethnic Hungarians were left outside the new borders.

The Hungarian People's Republic was established in 1949 as a satellite state inside the Warsaw Pact. The Hungarian Revolution of 1956 was unsuccessful, and during the Revolutions of 1989 the country moved peacefully to a democratic parliamentary republic. Parliament has 199 members.

The population was 9,689,000 in 2021, down from a peak of 10.8 million in 1980, and around 70% of the population lives in cities and towns, and a quarter of Hungarians live in the Budapest metropolitan area. About 5 million Hungarians live outside the country.
hussein-badreddin-al-houthi: Hussein al-Houthi was born on 20 August 1959 in the Marran area of northern Yemen, the ancestral home of the Houthi tribe; some sources give 1956 as the year. His father, Badreddin al-Houthi, was a prominent Zaydi cleric. According to a disciple, he lived for part of his life in Qom, in Iran, with his family, including his father and his younger brother Abdul-Malik; the same disciple claimed that he was close to Ali Khamenei, Supreme Leader of Iran, and to Hassan Nasrallah of Hezbollah.

He sat in the Yemeni parliament from 1993 to 1997 for Al-Haqq, the Party of Truth, a party of Zaydi and Shafi'i membership. When the party supported South Yemeni separatism it became a target of the government, and he fled, allegedly to Syria and then to Iran. After his return he broke with Al-Haqq. In 1990 or 1992 he founded the Believing Youth movement to teach young people about Zaydi Islam and its history and so to revive Zaydism in Saada Governorate.

The government of Ali Abdullah Saleh accused him of trying to set himself up as an imam, of opening unlicensed religious centres, of creating an armed group called Ansarallah and of staging violent protests against the United States and Israel. His followers held that the government was too closely allied with the United States.

On 18 June 2004 police arrested 640 of his followers who were demonstrating in front of the Great Mosque of Sanaa, and two days later the government offered a bounty of 55,000 US dollars for his capture and began an operation against him. In July the army killed 25 of his supporters and raised the bounty to 75,500 dollars. On 10 September the interior and defence ministries announced that he had been killed with 20 of his aides in Marran.

His father briefly took control of the movement after his death. The government buried him at the central prison of Sanaa so that his grave would not become a shrine. After Saleh stepped down, the new government handed his remains to his family on 28 December 2012, and on 5 June 2013 tens of thousands attended his reburial in Saada. His brothers Abdul-Malik, Yahia and Abdul-Karim are leaders of the movement.
